details:
**Diyas**
Small clay oil lamps lit in rows in homes, temples, and streets during Diwali, which is why it is called the "festival of lights." The holiday's other name, Deepavali, means "row of lamps." The lamps symbolize the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and they are said to light the way home for Rama and to welcome Lakshmi.

**Rangoli**
Colorful decorative patterns drawn on floors and doorsteps, often in circular or radial designs, using colored powder, chalk, rice, sand, or flower petals. They are made to welcome guests and the goddess Lakshmi into the home, and some households also draw small footprints in rice flour and vermilion to represent her entering.

**Lakshmi and Lakshmi Puja**
Lakshmi is the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, and Diwali celebrates her birth from the churning of the Ocean of Milk. The Lakshmi Puja, the main worship of the festival, takes place on the third and central day, when families clean their homes and light lamps so she will visit, offer her sweets, and often worship Ganesha as well. People also make major purchases, such as new clothes, in her honor.

**Rama and Sita's return to Ayodhya**
The most common story behind Diwali comes from the epic Ramayana: the prince Rama returned to his kingdom of Ayodhya with his wife Sita (and his brother Lakshmana) after 14 years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana. The people of Ayodhya lit lamps to welcome them home, a custom Diwali's diyas recall.

**Bhai Duj**
The fifth and final day of Diwali, which celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters; it is also called Bhaubeej, Bhai Tika, or Yama Dvitiya. Brothers visit their sisters' homes, where sisters pray for their well-being and feed them, and brothers give gifts in return. It is linked to the stories of the death god Yama visiting his sister Yamuna and of Krishna visiting his sister Subhadra.

**Narakasura and Naraka Chaturdashi**
The second day of Diwali, Naraka Chaturdashi (also called Choti Diwali), celebrates the slaying of the demon Narakasura, usually credited to Krishna, which freed the many people he held captive. In southern India, it is marked by an early-morning ritual oil bath, often with sesame oil.

**Bandi Chhor Divas**
The Sikh holiday celebrated at the same time as Diwali, meaning "Day of Liberation." It commemorates the release of the sixth Sikh Guru, Hargobind, from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. The Guru insisted that 52 imprisoned princes be freed with him, and he returned to Amritsar on Diwali.

**Mahavira's nirvana**
Jains celebrate Diwali as the anniversary of Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara, attaining final liberation (moksha or nirvana) on the new moon night of Kartik. The following day begins the Jain new year.

**Dhanteras**
The first day of Diwali, when people traditionally buy new utensils, metal goods, and gold as a sign of good fortune. It honors Dhanvantari, the god of medicine and Ayurveda, who emerged from the Ocean of Milk carrying the nectar of immortality. A legend also tells how the wife of King Hima's son saved him from death by keeping him awake with lamps and treasures, so that Yama, coming as a snake, was dazzled and left.

**Annakut and Padwa**
The fourth day of Diwali, which marks the start of the Hindu month of Kartik and the new year in many regions. Annakut ("mountain of food") or Govardhan Puja recalls Krishna lifting Govardhan Hill, and devotees offer mounds of food and sometimes build small hills of cow dung decorated with flowers. Padwa celebrates the bond between husband and wife, and husbands give gifts to their wives.

**Tihar**
The Nepali version of Diwali, a five-day festival celebrated by Hindus and Buddhists. Each day honors a different being: Kukur Tihar, the second day, honors dogs with garlands and food, and garlands of globe amaranth flowers are used in rituals such as Bhai Tika. Among the Newar people, the festival also includes Swanti.

**Kali Puja**
In West Bengal and other parts of eastern India, people worship the fierce goddess Kali on the Diwali new moon night instead of, or alongside, Lakshmi.

**Month of Kartik and the merchants' new year**
Diwali's main day falls on the new moon (amavasya), the darkest night, in the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, usually in October or November. Many Hindu merchants and business owners, especially Gujaratis and Marwaris, begin their new financial year at Diwali and open new account books.

**Mithai**
Sweets, such as barfi, ladoo, and sandesh, that are offered to Lakshmi in puja and exchanged as gifts with family and friends. Eating and sharing large amounts of sweets is one of the most characteristic customs of the festival.

**Firecrackers**
Fireworks and firecrackers are set off widely during Diwali, which causes severe air and noise pollution in Indian cities. In 2015, the Supreme Court of India declined to impose a complete ban on firecrackers during the festival, although later rulings restricted their use.
